headline: Trump and Xi seek stability despite disputes

sources.title: Trump and Xi see tensions flare over AI, trade and Iran but still seek stability (Associated Press)
Trump-Xi summit: Here's what's on the agenda, and why it matters (Al Jazeera)
Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun's Regular Press Conference on September 21, 2026 (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People's Republic of China)

chunks.text: Chinese President Xi Jinping began a three-day [[state visit]] to Washington on September 23, 2026. It is his first visit in 10 years and his third meeting with President Donald Trump in less than a year. Neither side expects major deals. Both leaders hope to {{smooth over}} tensions and steady [[fragile ties]]. Their countries have {{pulled back from}} last year's [[trade war]] and its very high [[tariffs]].

verbs.correct: To make a disagreement less serious
verbs.wrong: To announce a decision to the public
verbs.why: A good manager can smooth over a fight between two workers. A quick apology often smooths over an argument between friends. Trump and Xi hope to smooth over tensions during Xi's state visit to Washington.

verbs.correct: To stop being involved in something
verbs.wrong: To move ahead of a rival in a contest
verbs.why: Many investors pulled back from the housing market last year. The company pulled back from the deal when its costs rose. Washington and Beijing have pulled back from last year's trade war and its very high tariffs.

chunks.text: AI has become a major area of rivalry. The U.S. restricts exports of the most powerful [[AI chips]] to China. It accuses Chinese developers of {{tapping into}} American AI models to copy their abilities. Beijing {{pushes back}}, saying this practice, called [[distillation]], is widely used, including by American companies. It says Washington wants to [[monopolize]] the industry. Still, the U.S. has proposed {{setting up}} a warning system for AI incidents that could affect [[national security]].

verbs.correct: To get access to a resource and use it
verbs.wrong: To warn someone in secret about a plan
verbs.why: Small towns can tap into state money to fix their roads. Students can tap into the library's online collection from home. Washington accuses Chinese developers of tapping into American AI models to copy their abilities.

verbs.correct: To argue against a claim or plan
verbs.why: Parents often push back when a school changes its hours. Workers may push back against a new rule they think is unfair. Beijing pushes back against American claims, saying distillation is widely used, including by American companies.

verbs.correct: To create a new system or group
verbs.wrong: To save money for a later purpose
verbs.why: A city can set up a hotline for storm warnings. Neighbors often set up a group chat to share local news. Washington has proposed setting up a warning system for AI incidents that could affect national security.

chunks.text: Both governments have {{held back}} from big moves that would break their [[trade truce]]. This year, the U.S. Supreme Court {{struck down}} Trump's tariffs on [[trading partners]]. In July, the White House {{rolled out}} a 12.5 percent tariff on 60 countries, including China, over [[forced labor]] concerns. Last year, China {{choked off}} supplies of [[critical minerals]]. China's foreign ministry now says it wants those [[supply chains]] to stay "safe and stable."

verbs.correct: To stop yourself from doing something
verbs.wrong: To present something as an example
verbs.why: A shy student may hold back from asking questions in class. The fans held back from cheering until the result was official. Both governments have held back from big moves that would break their trade truce.

verbs.correct: To cancel a law or rule officially
verbs.wrong: To begin a friendship or talk
verbs.why: A judge can strike down a law that goes against the constitution. The state's top court struck down the new voting map. This year, the Supreme Court struck down Trump's tariffs on trading partners.

verbs.correct: To introduce a new policy or plan
verbs.wrong: To lower tariffs to an earlier level
verbs.why: The bank will roll out a new savings plan next month. The state rolled out a plan to repair old bridges. In July, the White House rolled out a 12.5 percent tariff on 60 countries, including China.

verbs.correct: To stop a supply of something
verbs.why: A long strike can choke off the supply of goods to stores. Heavy snow choked off food deliveries to the mountain town. Last year, China choked off supplies of critical minerals during the trade war.

chunks.text: The Trump administration wants to {{cut off}} Iran from its trading partners. Beijing insists on its right to trade with Tehran. China, Iran's biggest oil buyer, has been {{building up}} payment channels outside the U.S.-led [[financial system]], an economist said. Taiwan, a [[self-governing]] island that Beijing claims, is another [[thorny issue]]. After visiting Beijing in May, Trump paused a large [[weapons package]] for Taiwan. U.S. law requires Washington to help the island defend itself. Analysts expect Xi to press Trump to keep {{putting off}} [[arms sales]].

verbs.correct: To stop someone's links with others
verbs.why: Sanctions can cut off a country from world banks. A flood cut off the town from nearby cities for a week. The Trump administration wants to cut off Iran from its trading partners.

verbs.correct: To develop something little by little
verbs.wrong: To include something from the start
verbs.why: A new shop needs years to build up a loyal group of customers. Athletes build up strength with daily training. An economist said China has been building up payment channels outside the U.S.-led financial system.

verbs.wrong: To suggest an idea for discussion
verbs.why: Many people put off going to the dentist. The school put off the field trip because of bad weather. Analysts expect Xi to press Trump to keep putting off arms sales to Taiwan.

mainIdea.s: Xi is making his first visit to Washington in ten years, and both leaders want calmer ties. Still, their governments keep competing over AI, tariffs, Iran and Taiwan.
mainIdea.why: Xi's state visit is his first in 10 years, and both leaders hope to smooth over tensions. Their governments still compete hard on several fronts.

mainIdea.s: Xi's first trip to the U.S. capital in a decade comes as both sides seek steadier relations. China restricts exports of AI chips, and the U.S. says distillation is common.
mainIdea.why: Close, but it is the U.S. that restricts exports of powerful AI chips to China. Beijing is the side that says distillation is widely used.

mainIdea.s: Leaders of the two countries met at the United Nations to sign a new climate deal. They promised to burn less coal and share clean energy technology with poorer nations.
mainIdea.why: There was no climate deal at the United Nations. Xi began a state visit to Washington amid disputes over AI, trade, Iran and Taiwan.

lines.text: Did you hear that Xi Jinping is in Washington this week?
I did. It's his first trip there in 10 years, isn't it?
Yes. Both leaders say they want stability, so they're trying to {{smooth over}} tensions.
[[All smiles in public]], I bet. But what do they actually disagree about?
AI, mostly. The U.S. limits sales of the most powerful chips to China.
And Washington says Chinese developers are {{tapping into}} American AI models.
It does, but Beijing {{pushes back}}. It says American companies use the same method.
So is there any good news at all?
A little. The U.S. has proposed {{setting up}} a warning system for AI incidents.
[[Baby steps]]. What about trade? Weren't they in a trade war last year?
They were, but they've {{pulled back from}} that fight. Both sides have also {{held back}} from moves that would break the truce.
Didn't the White House {{roll out}} a new tariff this summer, though?
In July, yes. That came after the Supreme Court {{struck down}} the earlier tariffs. There are [[a lot of moving parts]].
And Iran? That sounds even harder.
Washington wants to {{cut off}} Iran from its trading partners, but Beijing says it has the right to trade with Tehran.
Sounds like they'll have to [[agree to disagree]] on that one.
Probably. Analysts also expect Xi to press Trump to {{put off}} arms sales to Taiwan.
So both leaders are [[walking a tightrope]]. Friendly enough to talk, but still rivals.

expressions.def: Used to say that people look friendly in front of others, even when they disagree in private
ex: The two coaches were all smiles in public after their argument.
The rivals shook hands and stayed all smiles in public.

expressions.def: Used to say that a small amount of progress still counts as progress
ex: They agreed to meet again next month. Baby steps.
He walked to the corner and back today. Baby steps.

expressions.def: Used to say that a situation has many pieces that all affect each other
ex: The new budget has a lot of moving parts.
Planning a wedding means a lot of moving parts.

expressions.def: To accept that two sides have different views and stop trying to change each other's minds
ex: We will never like the same music, so let's agree to disagree.
The two neighbors agreed to disagree about the fence.

expressions.def: Trying to keep a careful balance in a difficult situation
ex: The mayor is walking a tightrope between the two groups.
Parents of teenagers are always walking a tightrope.
